questions.q: When a question asks for 'two' details, you should
questions.why: Extra points can be ignored or count against you.

questions.q: Skimming a text means
o: reading quickly for the general idea
questions.why: Scanning is looking for specific information.

questions.q: A question asks for one detail. What is best?
o: A short, precise answer taken from the text
questions.why: Read the question carefully: extra wrong details can cancel a right one.

questions.q: Read: 'The museum is open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., except on Mondays, when it closes at 1 p.m. Entry is free for children under 12.' When does the museum close on a Monday?
o: It does not open on Mondays
questions.why: The text says that on Mondays 'it closes at 1 p.m.'. The 5 p.m. closing time applies to the other days, which is the detail a careless reader might pick.

questions.q: Scanning a text means
o: reading every sentence slowly to understand it fully
looking quickly through the text for a specific piece of information
reading only the title and guessing the content
rewriting the text in your own words
questions.why: Scanning is searching for something particular, such as a date, name or number. Reading quickly for the general idea is skimming.

long.q: Read the text and answer the questions. 'Community gardens are spreading in many cities. In Riverside, a group of neighbours turned an empty car park into a garden in 2019. Volunteers meet every Saturday morning to plant vegetables, and anything they grow is given free to a local food bank. Organiser Maya Patel says the biggest benefit is not the food but the friendships: "People who had lived on the same street for twenty years had never spoken before." The project now plans to add a small classroom so that local schools can visit.' (a) What was the site before it became a garden? (b) When do the volunteers meet? (c) What happens to the food they grow? (d) According to Maya Patel, what is the biggest benefit of the garden? (e) What does the project plan to do next?
scheme: B1: (a) an (empty) car park
B1: (b) (every) Saturday morning
B1: (c) it is given free to a (local) food bank
B1: (d) the friendships / neighbours getting to know each other (not 'the food')
B1: (e) add a (small) classroom (for school visits)
long.ans: a car park; Saturday mornings; given free to a food bank; the friendships; add a classroom

long.q: Read the text and answer the questions. 'When she was fourteen, Amara Diallo noticed that her grandmother struggled to carry water from the village well, 800 metres from home. Using an old bicycle wheel, a plastic barrel and some wood, Amara built a rolling water carrier that holds 50 litres – five times what her grandmother could carry in a bucket. Her design won a national science prize in 2022, and the £2,000 prize money paid for twenty more carriers for families in her village. Amara, now seventeen, hopes to study engineering at university. “I didn't invent anything difficult,” she says. “I just looked carefully at a problem.”' (a) How far was the well from Amara's home? (b) Name two materials Amara used. (c) How much water could her grandmother carry in a bucket? (d) What did Amara do with the prize money? (e) What does Amara want to study? (f) According to Amara, what was the key to her success?
scheme: B1: (a) 800 metres
B1: (b) two of: a bicycle wheel / a plastic barrel / wood
B1: (c) 10 litres (50 ÷ 5)
B1: (d) paid for twenty more carriers for families in her village
B1: (e) engineering
B1: (f) looking carefully at a problem (not inventing something difficult)
long.ans: 800 metres; e.g. bicycle wheel and plastic barrel; 10 litres; paid for 20 more carriers; engineering; looking carefully at a problem

long.q: Read the advertisement and answer the questions. 'Lakeside Adventure Camp – Summer 2026. Ages 11–15. Week-long courses from 20 July to 28 August. Activities: kayaking, climbing, archery and night hikes. All equipment provided; bring a sleeping bag and a torch. Price: $350 per week, or $300 if you book before 1 May. Brothers and sisters each receive a further 10% discount. Campers who cannot swim must take a free swimming test on the first morning before joining water activities.' (a) Who is the camp for? (b) What must campers bring? (c) How much does one week cost if you book in March? (d) Two sisters book one week each in June. How much do they pay altogether? (e) What must campers who cannot swim do?
scheme: B1: (a) young people aged 11–15
B1: (b) a sleeping bag and a torch (both needed)
B1: (e) take a (free) swimming test on the first morning before water activities
long.ans: ages 11–15; sleeping bag and torch; $300; $630; a swimming test on the first morning

long.q: Read what four people say about learning a language, then answer the questions. A – Kenji: 'I learned Spanish mainly from watching football commentary. At first I understood nothing, but after a year I could follow every match.' B – Fatima: 'My company paid for evening classes in German. The teacher was strict, but the grammar practice was exactly what I needed for my job.' C – Lucas: 'I moved to Seoul without speaking any Korean. Ordering food was a daily challenge, and I made embarrassing mistakes, but my neighbours were patient.' D – Priya: 'I use an app for fifteen minutes every morning on the train. It's not perfect, but it keeps me practising when I'm busy.' Which person (A, B, C or D): (a) learned for work reasons? (b) learned by living in the country? (c) used a hobby to learn? (d) studies during a journey? (e) was taught by someone strict? (f) admits their method has weaknesses?
scheme: B1: (a) B
B1: (b) C
B1: (c) A
B1: (d) D
B1: (e) B
B1: (f) D
long.ans: B; C; A; D; B; D

long.q: Read the news report and answer the questions. 'A dog that went missing during a family holiday in the mountains has been found 300 kilometres away, three months later. Biscuit, a four-year-old collie, ran off when fireworks frightened her near the town of Belmont in March. Despite search parties and posters, there was no sign of her. In June, a farmer spotted a thin, muddy dog among his sheep and took her to a vet, who scanned her microchip. “We had almost given up hope,” said owner Tom Reyes, who drove through the night to collect her. Biscuit is now recovering well, although she still hides whenever she hears a loud bang.' (a) How old is Biscuit? (b) What made Biscuit run away? (c) Give one thing the family did to try to find her. (d) How did the vet identify Biscuit? (e) How long was Biscuit missing? (f) What shows that Biscuit is still affected by her experience?
scheme: B1: (a) four (years old)
B1: (b) fireworks frightened her
B1: (c) search parties or posters
B1: (d) by scanning her microchip
B1: (e) three months
B1: (f) she hides when she hears a loud bang
long.ans: four; fireworks; search parties / posters; scanned her microchip; three months; she hides at loud bangs

questions.q: Good notes are
o: brief points under the given headings
full sentences copied from the text
questions.why: Notes should be short and relevant to each heading.

questions.q: In note-making, what should notes be?
o: Full sentences copied from the text
Brief points under the headings given
questions.why: Each note should be a separate, relevant point.

questions.q: What is lost if two notes say the same thing?
o: The second note earns no extra mark
questions.why: Make every note a different point.

questions.q: Under the heading 'Reasons people visit the park', which is the best note?
o: The park was opened by the mayor in 1998.
I think the park is a lovely place to visit.
The park is a place which many people say that they like to go to because it is very quiet.
questions.why: A good note is brief and answers the heading. The second does not give a reason, the third is an opinion, and the fourth is a long sentence rather than a note.

questions.q: The text says: 'Volunteers clean the beach every month, and they also teach children about recycling.' How should this appear in notes under 'What volunteers do'?
o: One note: volunteers do things to help
Two separate notes: clean the beach monthly; teach children about recycling
One note copying the whole sentence
No note, because it is about volunteers
questions.why: The sentence contains two different activities, so each can earn its own mark as a separate note. A vague note like 'do things to help' is too general to be credited.

long.q: Read the text and make notes under two headings: 'Benefits of cycling to school' (two notes) and 'Problems' (two notes). 'More students at Greenhill School now cycle to school. Cycling is cheaper than taking the bus, and many students say they arrive feeling more awake. It also reduces traffic outside the school gates at 8 a.m. However, there are not enough bike racks, so some bicycles are left against walls, and parents worry about a busy road junction near the school. In winter, rain and dark mornings also put some students off.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a benefit: any of cheaper than the bus / arrive more awake / less traffic at the gates
B1: a second, different benefit from that list
B1: a problem: any of too few bike racks / busy junction (safety) / rain and dark winter mornings
B1: a second, different problem from that list

long.q: Read the text and make notes under two headings: 'Advantages of e-scooters' (three notes) and 'Concerns' (three notes). 'Electric scooters have appeared in many cities in the past five years. Users like them because they are quick for short journeys and cheaper than taxis. They produce no exhaust fumes, which helps reduce air pollution in busy centres, and they can be left at many points around the city. However, injuries among riders have risen, partly because many do not wear helmets. Pedestrians complain that scooters left on pavements are a trip hazard, especially for blind people, and some riders break the law by using them on footpaths.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: an advantage: any of quick for short journeys / cheaper than taxis / no exhaust fumes (less air pollution) / can be left at many points
B1: a second, different advantage from that list
B1: a third, different advantage from that list
B1: a concern: rising injuries to riders (many without helmets)
B1: a concern: scooters left on pavements are a trip hazard (especially for blind people)
B1: a concern: riders illegally using footpaths

long.q: Read the text and make notes under two headings: 'Before the interview' (three notes) and 'At the interview' (three notes). 'Preparation is the key to a successful job interview. Find out as much as you can about the company beforehand by reading its website, and think of two or three questions to ask the interviewer. Plan your journey so that you arrive ten minutes early. On the day itself, make eye contact and give a firm handshake. When you answer questions, give real examples of things you have done rather than simply saying you are hard-working. Finally, remember to thank the interviewer at the end.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: before: research the company (read its website)
B1: before: prepare two or three questions to ask
B1: before: plan the journey to arrive ten minutes early
B1: at: make eye contact and give a firm handshake
B1: at: give real examples of what you have done
B1: at: thank the interviewer at the end

long.q: Read the text and make notes under three headings: 'How mangroves help people' (two notes), 'Threats to mangroves' (two notes) and 'What is being done' (one note). 'Mangrove forests grow along tropical coastlines where the land meets the sea. Their tangled roots protect coastal villages from storm waves and erosion, and they provide a nursery for young fish, which supports local fishing families. Mangroves also store large amounts of carbon. Yet they are disappearing: many have been cleared for shrimp farms and hotels, and plastic waste is choking young trees. In several countries, community groups are now replanting mangrove seedlings, and some governments have made it illegal to cut them down.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: help: protect villages from storm waves and erosion
B1: help: a nursery for young fish, supporting fishing families (or: store carbon)
B1: threat: cleared for shrimp farms and hotels
B1: threat: plastic waste choking young trees
B1: action: replanting seedlings, or laws against cutting them down

long.q: Read the text and make notes under two headings: 'Reasons to learn to cook' (three notes) and 'How schools could help' (two notes). 'Many young people leave home without knowing how to cook a simple meal. Learning to cook saves money, since home-made food is far cheaper than takeaways, and it usually leads to a healthier diet with more vegetables and less salt. Cooking for friends can also be a sociable, confidence-building experience. Some experts believe schools should do more: they suggest compulsory cookery lessons up to age 14 and after-school clubs where students prepare meals to take home to their families.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: reason: saves money (cheaper than takeaways)
B1: reason: a healthier diet (more vegetables, less salt)
B1: reason: sociable and builds confidence
B1: schools: compulsory cookery lessons up to age 14
B1: schools: after-school clubs where students cook meals to take home

questions.q: A summary should be written
o: in your own words, as one paragraph within the word limit
questions.why: Continuous, concise prose is expected.

questions.q: What should a summary include?
o: The relevant points, in your own words and in the word limit
questions.why: Organise points logically.

questions.q: Why keep to the word limit?
o: Long summaries are penalised and lose focus
questions.why: Plan the points first.

questions.q: Which sentence would be most useful in a summary of the advantages of learning online?
o: Students can study at any time and at their own speed.
My cousin took an online course last year.
Online learning was first developed several decades ago.
In conclusion, I strongly believe everyone should learn online.
questions.why: It states relevant advantages concisely. The others are an anecdote, an irrelevant historical fact and a personal opinion, none of which belong in a summary.

questions.q: The text says: 'Walking to school is free, it keeps you fit, and it means you do not depend on buses that are often late.' Which is the best summary in your own words?
o: Walking to school is free, it keeps you fit, and you do not depend on buses.
Walking costs nothing, improves health and avoids unreliable public transport.
I prefer walking to school because buses are always late.
questions.why: It keeps all three points concisely and in new words. The first copies the original, the second loses the points, and the fourth adds a personal opinion.

long.q: Read the text, then write a summary of the benefits of part-time jobs for teenagers. Write about 80 words, using your own words as far as possible. 'Many teenagers take part-time jobs while they are still at school. Earning their own money teaches them how to budget, and many say they value things more when they have paid for them themselves. Jobs in shops or cafés also build confidence, because young workers must speak to customers and solve problems quickly. Employers say that teenagers who have worked are often more reliable and punctual later in life. Some students also discover what kind of career they would like, or would not like, through these jobs. Critics point out, though, that working too many hours can leave students tired in lessons.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: they learn to budget / manage money
B1: they value things more when they have paid for them
B1: they gain confidence (dealing with customers, solving problems)
B1: they become more reliable and punctual
B1: they find out which careers they would (or would not) like
B1: own words, about 80 words, and no drawbacks included (tiredness is not a benefit)

long.q: Read the text, then write a summary of the reasons why families are moving from cities to small towns. Write about 80 words, using your own words as far as possible. 'Since 2020, thousands of families have left big cities for small towns. The most common reason is the cost of housing: a flat in the capital can cost the same as a large house with a garden in the countryside. Remote working has made the move possible, as many people now only need to visit the office once or twice a week. Parents also mention smaller class sizes in rural schools and the freedom for children to play outside safely. Others simply want a slower pace of life, away from traffic and crowds. However, some newcomers find that poor internet connections and limited public transport make country life harder than they expected.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: housing is cheaper, so families get more space for their money
B1: remote working means they rarely need to go to the office
B1: smaller classes in rural schools
B1: children can play outside safely
B1: a slower, calmer life without traffic and crowds
B1: own words, about 80 words, and no drawbacks (internet, transport) included

long.q: Read the text, then write a summary of the difficulties faced by students who go to university abroad. Write about 80 words, using your own words as far as possible. 'Studying abroad is exciting, but many students find the first months difficult. Homesickness is common, especially during festivals when families gather at home. Everyday tasks, such as opening a bank account or registering with a doctor, can be confusing in a new system and a new language. Some students struggle with a different style of teaching, where they are expected to question their lecturers and work independently. Money is another worry: rents in university cities are often high, and part-time work may be limited by visa rules. Most universities now offer support, including welcome weeks and student mentors.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: homesickness, especially at festival times
B1: everyday tasks (banking, seeing a doctor) are confusing in an unfamiliar system and language
B1: a different teaching style that expects independence and questioning
B1: high rents / money worries
B1: visa rules limit part-time work
B1: own words, about 80 words, and the support offered by universities not included

long.q: Read the text, then write a summary of the measures Vesterby took to reduce traffic. Write about 80 words, using your own words as far as possible. 'Ten years ago, the centre of Vesterby was choked with traffic. Today, it is one of the quietest towns in the region. The council began by closing the main square to cars and turning it into a pedestrian zone with cafés and benches. It then built a network of protected cycle lanes and offered free bicycle repairs on Saturdays. Bus fares were cut by half for under-18s and over-65s, and new car parks were built on the edge of town, with electric shuttle buses running to the centre every ten minutes. Shopkeepers were worried at first, but most now report more customers than before.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: the main square closed to cars and made pedestrian-only
B1: protected cycle lanes built
B1: free bike repairs on Saturdays
B1: half-price bus fares for under-18s and over-65s
B1: car parks built on the edge of town
B1: electric shuttle buses to the centre every ten minutes
B1: own words, about 80 words, and the shopkeepers' reaction not included

long.q: Read the text, then write a summary of the reasons why board games have become popular again. Write about 80 words, using your own words as far as possible. 'Board games are enjoying a surprising comeback. Sales have risen every year for the past decade, and board-game cafés, where customers pay a small fee to play from a library of games, have opened in many cities. Fans say that games bring people together face to face, offering a break from screens. Modern games are also far more varied than the classics: some are cooperative, with players working together against the game rather than against each other. Others tell a story that unfolds over many sessions. For parents, games are a way to spend time with children without arguments about phones. Some players, however, complain that the best new games are expensive.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: they bring people together in person
B1: a break from screens
B1: more variety, e.g. cooperative games where players work together
B1: games with a story that continues over many sessions
B1: family time with children without arguments about phones
B1: own words, about 80 words, with no evidence of popularity (sales, cafés) or drawbacks (cost) included

questions.q: Which is the most suitable opening for an email to a friend?
questions.why: Informal register for a friend.

questions.q: Which tone suits an email to a friend?
questions.why: Match register to the reader.

questions.q: What must an informal email cover?
o: All three bullet points in the task
questions.why: Develop each point.

questions.q: Which is the most suitable ending for an email to a friend?
o: I look forward to receiving your prompt reply.
Can't wait to see you next week! Love, Ana
questions.why: A warm, personal ending suits a friend. 'Yours faithfully' and the formal request belong in formal letters, and 'the Management' is impersonal.

questions.q: Which sentence best develops a point in an email telling a friend about a school trip?
o: The best part was the boat ride, because we saw dolphins jumping right next to us!
questions.why: It adds a specific detail and a reason, which is what 'developing' a point means. The others are short, general statements that give the reader nothing new.

long.q: Write an email (120–160 words) to a friend about a school event you helped to organise: what it was, what you did, and what you would do differently. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: all three points covered and developed
B1: friendly, informal register throughout
B1: well organised, with an opening and closing
B1: a range of accurate grammar and vocabulary

long.q: Your cousin is coming to stay with your family for a week. Write an email to your cousin (120–160 words) suggesting places to visit, telling them what to pack, and asking whether there is any food they don't eat. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: places to visit suggested and developed with reasons
B1: packing advice given with reasons (weather, activities)
B1: a natural question about food they don't eat
B1: friendly, informal register with a suitable opening and closing
B1: a range of accurate grammar and vocabulary within 120–160 words

long.q: A teacher who taught you in primary school has just retired. Write a letter to them (120–160 words) telling them what you have achieved since you left, thanking them for something specific, and inviting them to an event at your new school. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: achievements described with some detail
B1: thanks linked to a specific memory or lesson
B1: an invitation with clear details (what, when, where)
B1: a friendly but respectful register suited to a former teacher
B1: well organised and accurate within 120–160 words

long.q: You recently lost something important and a stranger returned it to you. Write an email to a friend (120–160 words) describing what happened, how you felt, and what you did to thank the stranger. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: a clear account of the loss and how the item came back
B1: feelings described and developed (panic, relief, gratitude)
B1: what you did to thank the stranger
B1: informal register, organised in paragraphs with an opening and closing
B1: a range of accurate past tenses and vocabulary within 120–160 words

long.q: Write an email to a pen friend in another country (120–160 words) describing a festival celebrated in your area: what happens, why it is important to you, and inviting them to come next year. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: what happens at the festival described with specific detail
B1: why it matters to you explained
B1: a warm invitation with practical details
B1: friendly, informal register throughout
B1: accurate, varied language within 120–160 words

questions.q: A report usually has
o: a title and clear sections or paragraphs with a recommendation
questions.why: Reports are organised for a reader to act on.

questions.q: Which phrase fits a formal register?
o: In my view, this proposal would benefit students.
questions.why: Formal writing avoids slang and contractions.

questions.q: Which is suitable for a report to a head teacher?
o: Formal language with clear headings or paragraphs
questions.why: Give recommendations where asked.

questions.q: In a review of a new restaurant for a school magazine, what should the final paragraph usually include?
o: A recommendation saying whether readers should go and why
A list of every dish on the menu
A greeting to the restaurant owner
questions.why: A review ends with an overall judgement and recommendation for the reader. Listing every dish adds no evaluation, and a greeting belongs in a letter.

questions.q: Which sentence is most suitable for an article in a school magazine encouraging students to join a club?
o: Join the club, it's mega cool lol.
Have you ever wanted to learn a new skill and make friends at the same time? The photography club could be for you.
Pursuant to the regulations, all students are required to attend.
The club exists. It is on Tuesdays.
questions.why: An article should engage the reader, for example with a direct question, in a lively but appropriate register. The others are too slangy, too legalistic, or flat and unengaging.

long.q: Your school wants to reduce plastic waste. Write a report for your headteacher (150–200 words) suggesting two ideas and recommending one. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: a clear title and purpose
B1: two ideas, each explained with a benefit
B1: a reasoned recommendation
B1: formal register, no slang
B1: accurate, varied language

long.q: Your school magazine is running a debate: 'Should every student do volunteer work?' Here are two comments: 'It teaches skills employers value.' 'Students are already too busy with schoolwork.' Write an article (150–200 words) giving your views. You may use these ideas and your own. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: both given ideas addressed and developed
B1: at least one idea of your own added
B1: article conventions: a title, an engaging opening, addresses the reader
B1: a register suited to the school magazine
B1: accurate, varied language within 150–200 words

long.q: Write a review (150–200 words) of a film or book you have enjoyed, for a website for teenagers. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: the work introduced (title, type, basic situation) without retelling the whole plot
B1: strengths evaluated with reasons
B1: a weakness, or who might not enjoy it
B1: a clear recommendation or rating
B1: an engaging register and accurate language within 150–200 words

long.q: Your town wants to attract more young visitors. Write a report (150–200 words) for the tourist office, suggesting two ideas and recommending one. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: report format: a title and an introduction stating the purpose
B1: a first idea explained with its benefit for young visitors
B1: a second idea explained with its benefit
B1: a reasoned recommendation
B1: formal register and accurate language within 150–200 words

long.q: Write an article (150–200 words) for your local newspaper called 'Why our town needs more green spaces'. Mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: at least two benefits explained, e.g. health, wildlife, cooler streets, places to meet
B1: specific local examples or suggestions
B1: a clear, persuasive viewpoint, with a possible objection answered
B1: an appropriate register for newspaper readers, with a title
B1: accurate, varied language within 150–200 words

questions.q: In a gap-fill listening task, your answer should usually be
o: one or two words heard in the recording
questions.why: Write the words you hear, spelled correctly.

questions.q: In the listening exam, what should you do before the recording starts?
o: Read the questions and note what information is needed
questions.why: Spelling of key words still matters.

questions.q: Answers in the listening exam should be:
o: Brief, as instructed, with key words spelled recognisably
questions.why: Listen for the specific detail asked for.

questions.q: In a listening task, the speaker says: 'The bus leaves at ten fifteen... sorry, I mean ten fifty.' What time should you write?
questions.why: Speakers often correct themselves, and the final corrected information is the answer. Writing both answers will not be credited.

questions.q: In a multiple-choice listening question, why must you listen to the whole section before choosing?
o: Because the answer is always in the last sentence
Because the recording is played only once
Because speakers often mention all the options, and only one matches what is actually meant
Because the questions are not in the same order as the recording
questions.why: Distractors are usually mentioned in the recording too, then rejected or changed, so choosing the first option you hear is a common mistake. The recording is in fact played twice, and questions follow its order.

long.q: Ask someone to read this aloud to you once while you don't look at it, then complete the notes with one or two words or a number. 'Hello everyone, and welcome to the Bayside Aquarium. Our tour today lasts about forty-five minutes. We'll start at the shark tunnel, which opened last year, and finish at the rock pool, where you can touch starfish. Please don't use flash photography, because it upsets the animals. The café is on the second floor and closes at four thirty. Finally, if you'd like to volunteer here, you must be at least sixteen.' Notes: Tour length: ___. First stop: ___. At the rock pool, visitors can touch ___. Not allowed: ___ photography. Café closes at ___. Minimum age for volunteers: ___. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: (about) 45 minutes
B1: (the) shark tunnel
B1: starfish
B1: flash
B1: 4.30 / four thirty
B1: 16 / sixteen

long.q: Ask someone to read this telephone message aloud to you twice while you don't look at it, then answer the questions. 'Hi, this is Carla from Westside Dental Clinic, calling for Mr Ahmed. I'm afraid we need to move your appointment on Thursday the twelfth. Dr Lee is away that day, so could you come on Friday the thirteenth at a quarter past ten instead? If that's not convenient, please ring us back on 0162 447 915 before five o'clock today. Oh, and please remember to bring your new insurance card. Thanks, bye.' (a) Who is the message for? (b) Why is the appointment being moved? (c) What is the new day and time? (d) What number should he ring? (e) By what time should he ring back? (f) What must he bring? (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: (a) Mr Ahmed
B1: (b) Dr Lee is away
B1: (c) Friday (the 13th) at 10.15
B1: (e) five o'clock (today)
B1: (f) his new insurance card
long.ans: Mr Ahmed; Dr Lee is away; Friday 13th, 10.15; 0162 447 915; 5 o'clock; new insurance card

long.q: Ask someone to read this radio interview aloud to you twice while you don't look at it, then answer the questions. 'Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Ravi Shah, who volunteers with the Highland Mountain Rescue team. Ravi, how did you get involved? Ravi: Well, I was a keen climber, and about eight years ago a friend of mine broke his ankle on a hill walk. The team that rescued him was so calm and professional that I decided to join. Interviewer: What does the training involve? Ravi: It takes about two years. We learn first aid, navigation in bad weather and how to use ropes to lower a stretcher safely. Interviewer: What's the most common call-out? Ravi: People think it's climbers falling, but actually it's walkers who get lost, usually because their phone battery has died and they were relying on it for maps. Interviewer: Any advice for listeners? Ravi: Always carry a paper map and a compass – and tell someone where you're going.' (a) Why did Ravi decide to join? [1] (b) How long does training take? [1] (c) Name two things volunteers learn. [2] (d) What is the most common reason for a call-out? [1] (e) Why does this usually happen? [1] (f) What two pieces of advice does Ravi give? [2] (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: (a) the team that rescued his friend was so calm and professional
B1: (b) about two years
B1: (c) one of: first aid / navigation in bad weather / using ropes to lower a stretcher
B1: (c) a second, different item from that list
B1: (d) walkers getting lost (not climbers falling)
B1: (e) their phone battery died and they relied on it for maps
B1: (f) carry a paper map and a compass
B1: (f) tell someone where you are going

long.q: Ask someone to read this talk aloud to you twice while you don't look at it, then complete the notes with one or two words or a number. 'Good afternoon. Today's talk is about the history of chocolate. People in Central America were drinking chocolate more than three thousand years ago, but it was a bitter drink, often flavoured with chilli. When cocoa reached Europe in the sixteenth century, sugar was added and it became fashionable among the rich. Solid chocolate bars were not made until 1847, by a company in Bristol, England. Today, around seventy per cent of the world's cocoa comes from West Africa, mainly Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. Sadly, many cocoa farmers earn very little, which is why some shoppers now look for the Fairtrade label.' Notes: Early chocolate drink tasted ___ and was often flavoured with ___. In Europe, people added ___. First solid bars made in: ___ (year). Most cocoa now comes from: ___. Label some shoppers look for: ___. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: bitter
B1: chilli
B1: sugar
B1: West Africa (accept Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana)
B1: Fairtrade
long.ans: bitter; chilli; sugar; 1847; West Africa; Fairtrade

long.q: Ask two people to read this conversation aloud to you while you don't look at it, then answer the questions. 'Anna: So, for our geography project, shall we do the river or the shopping centre? Ben: The river, definitely. We can measure the water speed at three places. Anna: Okay, but we'll need permission from Mr Clark to leave school. Ben: I'll email him tonight. When shall we go? Anna: Not Wednesday – I've got orchestra. How about Thursday after lunch? Ben: Fine. And we should take wellies – the bank was really muddy last time. Anna: Good idea. I'll bring my dad's tape measure, and you bring the stopwatch.' (a) Which topic do they choose? (b) At how many places will they measure the water speed? (c) Who will contact Mr Clark, and how? (d) Why can't Anna go on Wednesday? (e) When will they go? (f) What will Anna bring? (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: (a) the river
B1: (b) three
B1: (c) Ben, by email (tonight)
B1: (d) she has orchestra
B1: (e) Thursday after lunch
B1: (f) (her dad's) tape measure
long.ans: the river; three; Ben, by email; orchestra; Thursday after lunch; a tape measure

questions.q: In the speaking test it helps to
o: develop answers with reasons and examples
questions.why: Extended, relevant answers score best.

questions.q: In the speaking test, what helps most?
o: Extending answers with reasons and examples
questions.why: Respond naturally to the examiner's prompts.

questions.q: If you don't understand a question in the speaking test, you should:
o: Ask politely for it to be repeated
questions.why: Asking for clarification is natural communication.

questions.q: The examiner asks: 'Do you prefer reading books or watching films?' Which answer is best?
o: I usually prefer books, because I can imagine the characters myself, although I enjoy films with friends at the weekend.
questions.why: It gives a preference, a reason and a contrasting idea, showing range of language and the ability to develop an answer.

questions.q: Which phrase is most useful for giving yourself a moment to think in the speaking test?
o: That's an interesting question. Let me think...
I don't want to answer that.
Can I say it in my language?
questions.why: A natural 'thinking' phrase keeps the conversation going while you plan. The others end or avoid the discussion and lose communication marks.

long.q: Record yourself speaking for 2–3 minutes on: 'Is it better to grow up in a city or in the countryside?' Talk about transport and facilities, friendships and free time, the environment, and say which you'd choose and why. Then listen back and mark yourself with this scheme.
scheme: B1: every prompt developed with reasons or examples, not one-line answers
B1: both sides considered before a clear choice
B1: a range of accurate grammar and topic vocabulary (facilities, commute, peaceful, isolated)
B1: clear pronunciation and keeps going without long pauses

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.why: 'Since' with an ongoing situation takes the present perfect.

questions.q: 'Despite ___ tired, he finished the race.'
questions.why: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or -ing form.

questions.q: A synonym for 'reluctant' is
questions.why: Reluctant means not wanting to do something.

questions.q: Which conditional sentence is correct?
o: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If it will rain tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If it rains tomorrow, we stay at home yesterday.
If it would rain tomorrow, we will stay at home.
questions.why: In the first conditional, the 'if' clause uses the present simple and the main clause uses 'will'. 'Will' or 'would' in the 'if' clause is a common error.

questions.q: 'I'm really looking forward ___ you next week.'
questions.why: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by the -ing form: 'looking forward to seeing'.

long.q: Each sentence has one mistake. Rewrite it correctly. (a) She don't like coffee. (b) I have lived here since five years. (c) If I will see him, I will tell him. (d) He is more taller than his brother. (e) We discussed about the problem.
